title: Job's Three Friends
lead: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite came to comfort Job (Job 2:11), sat with him in silence for seven days, and then argued with him through three rounds of speeches that his suffering must come from sin. God's verdict at the end is that they did not speak rightly of him, as Job did, and Job prays for them (Job 42:7–9).

sections.b: All three come from lands east and south of Israel. Teman was a town or region of Edom famous for its wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8–9), and an Eliphaz is Esau's son in Genesis 36:10–11. Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Naamah has not been identified with certainty. They are sages of the East, the international world of wisdom to which the book of Job belongs.

The friends share one conviction: God is just, so suffering is a sign of sin and prosperity a sign of righteousness. Eliphaz appeals to a night vision and to the tradition of the fathers; Bildad to the wisdom of earlier generations; Zophar to God's hidden wisdom and to what has been known 'from ancient times'. Much of what they say is repeated elsewhere in Scripture, and Paul quotes Eliphaz (1 Corinthians 3:19, citing Job 5:13). Their error, in the book's judgment, is to apply the doctrine to Job and to treat his honest protest as impiety (Job 42:7).
